topics.name: Richard Feynman
topics.kicker: Quantum electrodynamics pioneer · Diagrams, bongos, and the _Challenger_ probe
topics.briefing: Richard Feynman was an American physicist who loved puzzles, practical jokes, and playing the bongo drums. He shared the 1965 Nobel Prize for quantum electrodynamics, the theory of how light and electrons interact, and he invented simple sketches, now called Feynman diagrams, to keep track of what particles do when they meet. In 1986, at a televised hearing, he showed how cold had stiffened the rubber O-rings that failed on the space shuttle _Challenger_.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In a 1959 talk titled “There’s Plenty of Room at the Bottom,” this physicist asked why the entire _Encyclopaedia Britannica_ could not be written on the head of a pin, an idea later credited with inspiring nanotechnology. He gave that talk at Caltech, where he taught for most of his career.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this American physicist who shared the 1965 Nobel Prize for quantum electrodynamics and drew famous diagrams of particle interactions.

tossups.p: This scientist wrote that “for a successful technology, reality must take precedence over public relations, for nature cannot be fooled,” in an appendix to a report on a 1986 disaster. He wrote it as a member of the Rogers Commission, set up by President Ronald Reagan.
tossups.r: At a televised hearing, he dunked a clamped O-ring sample in ice water to show that cold made it stiff. For 10 points, name this physicist who helped investigate the _Challenger_ disaster.

tossups.p: Freeman Dyson showed that this physicist’s approach to quantum electrodynamics matched the very different methods of Julian Schwinger and Sin-Itiro Tomonaga [“TOH-moh-NAH-gah”], who had worked out the same theory on their own. This physicist’s version relied on simple pictures, while Schwinger’s relied on pages of equations.
tossups.r: All three men shared the 1965 Nobel Prize in Physics. For 10 points, name this American physicist whose namesake diagrams show particles meeting and trading other particles.

tossups.p: This physicist described an antiparticle as an ordinary particle moving backward in time. In the sketches of particle collisions that he introduced in the late 1940s, a photon passing between two electrons is drawn as a wavy line.
tossups.r: Those sketches became known as diagrams named for him. For 10 points, name this American physicist who shared the 1965 Nobel Prize.

tossups.p: While working on the Manhattan Project at Los Alamos, this young physicist amused himself by cracking open his colleagues’ safes and filing cabinets. Stories like that one fill a best-selling 1985 book whose title begins _Surely You’re Joking_, which he told to his drumming partner, Ralph Leighton.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this bongo-playing physicist who won the 1965 Nobel Prize for quantum electrodynamics.

tossups.p: Three red volumes, edited with Robert Leighton and Matthew Sands, collect the lectures this man gave to beginning physics students at Caltech in the early 1960s. Those books, published in the 1960s, grew out of recordings of his classes.
tossups.r: This man also invented diagrams for drawing particle interactions. For 10 points, name this physicist who explained the _Challenger_ shuttle’s O-ring failure.

tossups.p: This physicist gave the name “partons” to tiny, pointlike pieces inside protons that explained late-1960s experiments at the Stanford Linear Accelerator, in which fast electrons bounced off protons. Partons were later identified as quarks and gluons.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Caltech physicist who shared the 1965 Nobel Prize and invented diagrams of particle interactions.

tossups.p: This physicist’s 1942 Princeton thesis, supervised by John Wheeler, led to his “sum over histories” method, which adds up every possible path a particle could take from one point to another. He taught at Cornell before spending the rest of his career at Caltech.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this physicist who shared the 1965 Nobel Prize for quantum electrodynamics.

tossups.p: In a 1974 commencement speech at Caltech, this scientist warned against “cargo cult science,” research that looks right on the surface but skips the honest testing that real science needs. In a 1981 talk, he suggested building computers that follow quantum rules in order to simulate nature.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this physicist known for his diagrams of particle interactions and his investigation of the _Challenger_ disaster.

tossups.p: A run of six 9s in a row that begins at the 762nd decimal place of pi is named for this physicist. His book _QED: The Strange Theory of Light and Matter_ explains, for ordinary readers, how light and electrons interact.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this American physicist who shared the 1965 Nobel Prize in Physics and played the bongo drums.

tossups.p: This physicist wrote the memoir _What Do You Care What Other People Think?_, whose title repeats a question his first wife, Arline, used to ask him. That book also describes his work on the Rogers Commission after a 1986 space disaster.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this physicist who used a glass of ice water to show why the space shuttle _Challenger_’s O-rings failed.

tossups.p: This physicist and two other men used a technique called renormalization to get rid of the infinite answers that had ruined calculations about how electrons and light interact. The theory they rescued, nicknamed QED, makes some of the most accurate predictions in all of science.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this American physicist who shared the 1965 Nobel Prize for that theory and drew famous particle diagrams.

tossups.p: A 1981 BBC television interview with this physicist was titled _The Pleasure of Finding Things Out_, a name later given to a book of his short works. In it, he described how his father taught him that knowing the name of a bird tells you nothing about how the bird actually behaves.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this American physicist, a Nobel winner, who played the bongos and invented diagrams of particle interactions.

tossups.p: With his Caltech colleague Murray Gell-Mann, this physicist worked out a 1958 theory of the weak nuclear force, the force behind beta decay. As a young man, this physicist earned his bachelor’s degree at MIT and his doctorate at Princeton.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this physicist who won the 1965 Nobel Prize and is known for his namesake diagrams.

tossups.p: In _The Character of Physical Law_, based on lectures he gave at Cornell, this physicist said, “I think I can safely say that nobody understands quantum mechanics.” Born in New York City in 1918 and raised in Queens, he became one of the most popular science teachers of his time.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this physicist who shared the 1965 Nobel Prize and helped investigate the _Challenger_ disaster.

clues.t: Shared the 1965 Nobel Prize in Physics for quantum electrodynamics (QED), the theory of how light and electrons interact
Invented the diagrams, named for him, that show particles meeting and trading other particles
Helped investigate the 1986 space shuttle _Challenger_ disaster; at a televised hearing, he dunked a clamped piece of O-ring in ice water
American physicist (1918–1988) from Queens, New York, famous for practical jokes and playing the bongo drums
Worked on the Manhattan Project at Los Alamos, where he cracked open colleagues’ safes for fun
Shared his Nobel Prize with Julian Schwinger and Sin-Itiro Tomonaga
Studied at MIT and Princeton, taught at Cornell, then spent the rest of his career at Caltech
His lectures to beginning Caltech students became three famous red volumes, edited with Robert Leighton and Matthew Sands
With drumming partner Ralph Leighton, told his life stories in a 1985 best seller whose title begins _Surely You’re Joking_ and in _What Do You Care What Other People Think?_
His _Challenger_ report appendix: “reality must take precedence over public relations, for nature cannot be fooled”
His 1959 talk “There’s Plenty of Room at the Bottom” asked why the whole _Encyclopaedia Britannica_ couldn’t fit on the head of a pin, inspiring nanotechnology
Freeman Dyson showed that his approach to QED matched Schwinger’s and Tomonaga’s
Used renormalization to remove the infinite answers that had ruined QED calculations
In his diagrams, a wavy line is a photon, and an antiparticle can be drawn as a particle moving backward in time
His 1942 Princeton thesis under John Wheeler led to the “sum over histories,” which adds up every path a particle could take
Named “partons,” the pointlike pieces inside protons that explained late-1960s electron experiments at Stanford; partons were later identified as quarks and gluons
With Murray Gell-Mann, worked out a 1958 theory of the weak nuclear force
Warned against “cargo cult science” in a 1974 Caltech commencement speech
In a 1981 talk, suggested building computers that follow quantum rules to simulate nature
A run of six 9s starting at pi’s 762nd decimal place is named for him
In _The Character of Physical Law_ (from lectures at Cornell): “I think I can safely say that nobody understands quantum mechanics”
His 1981 BBC interview _The Pleasure of Finding Things Out_ (later a book title) tells how his father taught him that a bird’s name tells you nothing about the bird
His book _QED: The Strange Theory of Light and Matter_ explains his theory for ordinary readers
k: strange theory of light and matter

trap.title: Not Schwinger or Oppenheimer
trap.body: This man shared his Nobel Prize with Julian Schwinger and Sin-Itiro Tomonaga, who worked out the same theory in different ways, and Freeman Dyson showed that all three approaches agreed. He also worked at Los Alamos under J. Robert Oppenheimer, and many tossups about the Manhattan Project or quantum electrodynamics mention several of these physicists together.
trap.fix: Diagrams, bongos, safecracking, the ice-water O-ring demonstration, partons, the “sum over histories,” and the red Caltech lecture books all mean this man. The director of the Los Alamos lab was Oppenheimer; the other two QED Nobel winners were Schwinger and Tomonaga. If a question asks for “these diagrams,” the answer is the diagrams, not the man.

topics.name: Heat capacity
topics.kicker: Heat needed to warm something one degree · Why water heats up so slowly
topics.dates: Studied by Joseph Black in the 1760s
topics.briefing: Heat capacity tells how much heat it takes to warm something up by one degree. Water’s value is unusually high, which is why a pot of water takes a while to boil, beach sand gets hot long before the ocean does, and coastal towns have milder weather than places far inland. Scientists often compare substances by their specific heat, the heat capacity of just one gram, and water’s is about 4.18 joules per gram per degree Celsius.
topics.answerHtml: Heat capacity (accept specific heat capacity, molar heat capacity, or thermal capacity; prompt on C; do not accept “latent heat”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The “lambda point” of helium, near 2.2 kelvins, is named for the Greek-letter shape that a graph of this quantity makes as helium turns into a superfluid. A metal’s value of this quantity jumps suddenly at the temperature where the metal becomes a superconductor.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, the amount of heat needed to raise an object’s temperature by one degree.

tossups.p: In 1819, Pierre Louis Dulong [“doo-LONG”] and Alexis Petit [“puh-TEE”] found that many solid elements have nearly the same value of this quantity per mole of atoms, about 25 joules per kelvin. Diamond’s value is far lower than that rule predicts at room temperature.
tossups.r: Water has an unusually high value of it. For 10 points, name this quantity measured in joules per kelvin, which tells how much heat it takes to warm something up.

tossups.p: Stars and black holes have negative values of this quantity, meaning they actually get hotter as they lose energy. Unlike its “specific” version, the ordinary version of this quantity depends on how much material an object contains. A full swimming pool has a far larger value of it than a cup of water.
tossups.r: Water has an unusually high value of it. For 10 points, name this quantity, the heat needed to raise an object’s temperature by one degree.

tossups.p: Sea breezes blow onshore on sunny afternoons partly because land has a lower value of this quantity than the ocean, so the land warms up faster. Coastal towns have milder summers and winters than inland towns because of water’s high value of this quantity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, the amount of heat needed to raise something’s temperature by one degree.

tossups.p: Students can find a metal’s value of this quantity per gram by dropping a hot sample into water inside a coffee-cup calorimeter and measuring how much the water warms. The formula Q equals m c delta T uses that per-gram value, symbolized lowercase c.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, which is unusually high for water and tells how much heat it takes to warm something up.

tossups.p: The food “Calorie” on nutrition labels is really a kilocalorie, and the original small calorie was chosen so that water’s value of this quantity per gram came out to exactly one. In joules, that per-gram value for water is about 4.18 per degree Celsius.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, the amount of heat needed to raise an object’s temperature by one degree.

tossups.p: Car engines are cooled with water-based coolant because water’s high value of this quantity lets it soak up a lot of heat while warming only a little. Water’s high value of this quantity comes from the energy needed to break its hydrogen bonds.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, measured in joules per kelvin, that tells how much heat it takes to warm something by one degree.

tossups.p: The speed of sound in a gas depends on the ratio of this quantity measured at constant pressure to this quantity measured at constant volume, a ratio called gamma. For a gas, the constant-pressure value of this quantity is always the larger one, because some of the added heat goes into pushing the gas outward.
tossups.r: Water has a high value of it. For 10 points, name this quantity, the heat needed to raise an object’s temperature by one degree.

tossups.p: On a heating curve, the slanted sections are less steep when a substance has a larger value of this quantity, while the flat sections show latent heat being absorbed during melting and boiling. Metals like copper have low values of this quantity, so they heat up quickly.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, which is unusually high for water and is measured in joules per kelvin.

tossups.p: Before using a calorimeter to measure a reaction, chemists find the calorimeter’s own value of this quantity, often called its “calorimeter constant.” Multiplying an object’s value of this quantity by its temperature change gives the heat it gained or lost.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, the heat needed to raise an object’s temperature by one degree.

tossups.p: In the 1760s, the Scottish chemist Joseph Black studied this quantity, and he also discovered latent heat. Black showed that equal masses of different substances need different amounts of heat to warm by the same number of degrees.
tossups.r: Water’s per-gram value of it is about 4.18 joules per degree Celsius. For 10 points, name this quantity, which is especially high for water.

tossups.p: Nitrogen gas has a larger value of this quantity per mole than argon does, because nitrogen’s two-atom molecules can also store energy by spinning. Helium and argon, both made of single atoms, have the same value of this quantity per mole.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, the amount of heat needed to raise an object’s temperature by one degree.

tossups.p: Thick adobe or stone walls have a large value of this quantity, so they keep desert homes cool during the hot day and warm through the cold night. Oceans store huge amounts of heat because of water’s large value of this quantity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, measured in joules per kelvin, which explains why beach sand heats up faster than the ocean.

tossups.p: Albert Einstein’s 1907 model of a solid treated its atoms as tiny vibrating springs to explain why this quantity shrinks at very low temperatures, and Peter Debye [“duh-BYE”] improved that model in 1912. Both models used the new quantum ideas of Max Planck.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, the amount of heat needed to warm an object by one degree.

tossups.p: Per gram, ice has only about half the value of this quantity that liquid water has, and steam also has about half of liquid water’s value. Builders use the term “thermal mass” for a large value of this quantity in materials like concrete and brick.
tossups.r: Its per-gram form is called “specific.” For 10 points, name this quantity, the heat needed to raise an object’s temperature by one degree.

clues.t: The amount of heat needed to raise an object’s temperature by one degree
Its “specific” version is per unit mass (per gram or kilogram); its “molar” version is per mole
Water’s value is unusually high: about 4.18 joules (1 calorie) per gram per degree Celsius
Explains why beach sand gets hot long before the ocean does
Measured in joules per kelvin; the per-mass version in joules per kilogram per kelvin (or joules per gram per degree Celsius)
Q = m c ΔT: heat equals mass times the per-gram value (lowercase c) times the temperature change
Measured with a calorimeter, like a coffee-cup calorimeter; a calorimeter’s own value is its “calorimeter constant”
Land’s lower value lets it warm faster than the sea, helping cause afternoon sea breezes and milder coastal climates
Metals like copper and iron have low values (copper’s per gram is less than a tenth of water’s), so they heat up fast
Depends on how much material there is: a swimming pool’s value is far larger than a cup of water’s
On a heating curve, a larger value makes the slanted sections less steep; the flat sections show latent heat
Water’s high value, from its hydrogen bonds, makes it a good coolant for car engines
Helium’s “lambda point,” near 2.2 K, is named for the λ shape its graph makes as helium becomes a superfluid
Dulong and Petit (1819): many solid elements have about 25 joules per kelvin per mole of atoms
Einstein’s 1907 model of vibrating atoms and Debye’s 1912 model explain why it drops toward zero for cold solids
Diamond’s value at room temperature is far below what the Dulong–Petit rule predicts
Stars and black holes have negative values: they get hotter as they lose energy
Scottish chemist Joseph Black studied it in the 1760s, showing that equal masses of different substances need different amounts of heat to warm equally; he also discovered latent heat
The constant-pressure value divided by the constant-volume value is gamma, which helps set the speed of sound in a gas
For a gas, the constant-pressure value is larger than the constant-volume value, since some heat goes into pushing the gas outward
Nitrogen gas has a larger value per mole than argon, because its two-atom molecules can also store energy by spinning; single-atom helium and argon share the same value per mole
A metal’s value jumps suddenly at the temperature where it becomes a superconductor
Per gram, ice and steam each have only about half of liquid water’s value
Builders call a large value “thermal mass”: thick adobe or stone walls keep desert homes cool by day and warm at night
The original small calorie was chosen so that water’s per-gram value is exactly 1 calorie per degree Celsius; a food Calorie is really a kilocalorie

trap.title: Not latent heat
trap.body: Heat capacity tells how much heat it takes to change an object’s temperature. Latent heat is the heat absorbed or released during a phase change, like melting or boiling, while the temperature does not change at all. Players also blurt out “temperature,” and some questions want only the “specific” version per gram, called specific heat, which is accepted here.
trap.fix: Warming by one degree, joules per kelvin, Q = m c ΔT, water’s 4.18, sea breezes, and calorimeters point to heat capacity or specific heat. Melting or boiling at a steady temperature, the flat parts of a heating curve, and heats of fusion or vaporization point to latent heat.
trap.line: Real answer line: Heat capacity (accept specific heat capacity, molar heat capacity, or thermal capacity; prompt on C; do not accept “latent heat”)

topics.name: Second law of thermodynamics
topics.kicker: Heat flows hot to cold on its own · Entropy never falls in an isolated system
topics.briefing: The second law of thermodynamics explains why hot cocoa cools down and ice melts in a warm room, but never the other way around: heat flows on its own from hot things to cold things, unless something does work to push it back. Another way to say it is that entropy, a measure of disorder, never decreases in an isolated system. It also means no engine can turn all of its heat into useful work, so even the best engine wastes some heat.
topics.answerHtml: Second law of thermodynamics (accept 2nd law of thermodynamics; prompt on second law or thermodynamics; do not accept “entropy” or another law)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In his 1959 lecture “The Two Cultures,” C. P. Snow said that being unable to describe this law was like never having read a work of Shakespeare. Arthur Eddington wrote that this law holds “the supreme position among the laws of Nature.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics, which says that the entropy of an isolated system never decreases.

tossups.p: A ship that ran by pulling heat out of the ocean and turning all of it into work would obey the conservation of energy but break this law. Lord Kelvin and Max Planck each gave a version of this law about engines like that one.
tossups.r: That version says no engine working in a cycle can turn heat entirely into work. For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics.

tossups.p: Refrigerators and air conditioners do not break this law, because they use electrical work to pump heat out of a cold space into a warmer room. Rudolf Clausius [“KLOW-zee-us”] published a famous statement of this law in 1854.
tossups.r: That statement says heat cannot pass on its own from a colder body to a warmer one. For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics.

tossups.p: Sadi Carnot [“kar-NOH”] laid groundwork for this law in his 1824 book _Reflections on the Motive Power of Fire_, which argued that a heat engine must always pass some heat on to a colder body. The most efficient possible engine runs on a cycle named for Carnot.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics, which says that no heat engine can be 100 percent efficient.

tossups.p: James Clerk Maxwell imagined a tiny “demon” that sorts fast and slow gas molecules between two boxes, which would seem to break this law by making one box hot and the other cold without doing any work. Physicists later showed that the demon’s need to record and erase information about the molecules would save this law.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics, which says that the entropy of an isolated system never decreases.

tossups.p: Ludwig Boltzmann [“BOHLTS-mahn”] explained this law with statistics: disordered arrangements of molecules vastly outnumber orderly ones, so a system almost always drifts toward disorder. This law gives time a one-way direction that Arthur Eddington called the “arrow of time.”
tossups.r: It explains why ice melts in a warm room. For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics, which says that entropy tends to increase.

tossups.p: In Isaac Asimov’s 1956 story “The Last Question,” people keep asking ever more powerful computers whether the effects of this law on the whole universe can ever be undone. Applied to the universe, this law suggests a far-future “heat death,” with no temperature differences left to power anything.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics, which explains why heat flows from hot objects to cold ones.

tossups.p: Erwin Schrödinger’s [“SHROH-ding-erz”] 1944 book _What Is Life?_ explored how living things stay organized despite this law. A living cell can lower the disorder inside itself only by giving off heat that raises the disorder of its surroundings even more, so life never breaks this law.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics, which says that the total entropy of an isolated system never decreases.

tossups.p: In a joke summary of the laws of thermodynamics, the first law says “you can’t win” and this law says “you can’t break even.” This law explains why a car engine must waste some of the energy in its fuel as heat.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics, which also says that heat flows on its own only from hot to cold.

tossups.p: In 1865, Rudolf Clausius [“KLOW-zee-us”] summed up thermodynamics in two rules, saying that the energy of the universe is constant and that its entropy tends toward a maximum. That same year, Clausius gave entropy its name.
tossups.r: The rule about entropy is this law. For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics, which says that heat flows on its own from hot to cold.

tossups.p: When the wall between a box of gas and an empty box is removed, the gas spreads through both boxes and never squeezes itself back into one, as this law predicts. The chance of all the molecules gathering back in one box by accident is so tiny that it never happens in practice.
tossups.r: Hot cocoa cools to room temperature because of this law. For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics, which says the entropy of an isolated system never decreases.

tossups.p: Max Planck wrote his 1879 doctoral thesis on this law. This law sets the best possible efficiency of a heat engine at one minus the ratio of its cold temperature to its hot temperature, measured in kelvins.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics, which says that entropy never decreases in an isolated system.

tossups.p: Jacob Bekenstein [“BEK-en-stine”] proposed a “generalized” version of this law that counts the entropy of black holes along with ordinary entropy. Stephen Hawking at first doubted Bekenstein, but then showed that black holes give off radiation.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics, which says that the total entropy of an isolated system never goes down.

tossups.p: A snowflake can grow into an orderly crystal without breaking this law, because the heat it gives off as it freezes raises the disorder of the air around it even more. Ice cubes can form in a freezer for a similar reason, since the freezer dumps even more heat into the kitchen.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics, which says heat flows on its own from hot to cold.

tossups.p: In 1851, William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, stated this law as the rule that no machine can get useful work out of an object just by cooling it below the temperature of its coldest surroundings. A perpetual-motion machine that kept running by recycling its own heat would break this law.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics, which says that no engine can be 100 percent efficient.

clues.t: Heat flows on its own from hot objects to cold ones, never the reverse, unless something does work to push it
The entropy (disorder) of an isolated system never decreases
No heat engine can be 100 percent efficient; some heat is always wasted
Explains why hot cocoa cools to room temperature and ice melts in a warm room, but never the reverse
Rudolf Clausius laid its foundation in 1850; his 1854 statement: heat cannot pass on its own from a colder body to a warmer one
William Thomson (Lord Kelvin), 1851: no machine can get work out of an object just by cooling it below its coldest surroundings
Kelvin–Planck statement: no engine working in a cycle can turn heat from one source completely into work
Refrigerators and air conditioners obey it by using electrical work to pump heat out of a cold space
Sadi Carnot’s 1824 _Reflections on the Motive Power of Fire_ laid its groundwork; the Carnot cycle is the most efficient possible engine
Joke summary of the laws of thermodynamics: the first says “you can’t win,” and this one says “you can’t break even”
The first law says energy is conserved; this one says which way energy naturally flows
Applied to the whole universe, it suggests a far-future “heat death” with no temperature differences left
Maxwell’s demon, an imaginary molecule-sorter, seemed to break it; the cost of recording and erasing the demon’s information saves it
C. P. Snow’s 1959 lecture “The Two Cultures”: not being able to describe it is like never having read Shakespeare
Arthur Eddington: it holds “the supreme position among the laws of Nature”; he called its one-way direction the “arrow of time”
Ludwig Boltzmann explained it with statistics: disordered arrangements vastly outnumber orderly ones
Clausius (1865), the year he named entropy: the energy of the universe is constant, and its entropy tends toward a maximum
Gas let into an empty box spreads through both boxes and never squeezes itself back into one; the odds are far too tiny
Best possible engine efficiency: one minus the cold temperature divided by the hot temperature, both in kelvins
Living things obey it by raising their surroundings’ disorder; Schrödinger’s 1944 book _What Is Life?_ explored this
Max Planck wrote his 1879 doctoral thesis on it
Jacob Bekenstein proposed a “generalized” version that also counts the entropy of black holes
In Isaac Asimov’s 1956 story “The Last Question,” people keep asking ever more powerful computers whether its effects on the universe can be undone
A ship powered only by pulling heat out of the ocean would obey the conservation of energy but break this law
A snowflake can grow into an orderly crystal because the heat it releases raises the surrounding air’s disorder even more; a freezer making ice dumps heat into the kitchen

trap.title: The law, not entropy
trap.body: Entropy is a quantity (disorder, symbolized S), and the second law of thermodynamics is the rule that entropy never decreases in an isolated system. If a question asks for “this law,” saying only “entropy” is wrong; if it asks for “this quantity,” the answer is entropy. Players also mix up which numbered law is which, and saying just “second law” earns only a prompt, since Newton and Kepler have second laws too.
trap.fix: Energy being conserved is the first law; absolute zero and perfect crystals are the third law; thermometers and thermal equilibrium are the zeroth law. Heat flowing hot to cold, engines that can’t be 100 percent efficient, Carnot, Clausius, Kelvin, and Maxwell’s demon point to the second law. Say the whole name: “second law of thermodynamics.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Second law of thermodynamics (accept 2nd law of thermodynamics; prompt on second law or thermodynamics; do not accept “entropy” or another law)

topics.name: Newton’s laws of motion
topics.kicker: Three rules of force and motion · Inertia, F = ma, and action–reaction
topics.briefing: Isaac Newton’s three laws of motion explain how forces change the way things move. The first says an object keeps doing what it is doing, staying still or moving in a straight line at a steady speed, unless a force acts on it; the second says force equals mass times acceleration; and the third says every action has an equal and opposite reaction. Newton published them in 1687 in the _Principia_, and they explain everything from seatbelts to rocket launches.
topics.answerHtml: Newton’s laws of motion (accept laws of motion; do not accept “Isaac Newton” or a single law, such as “inertia”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1920, a newspaper editorial mocked Robert Goddard by claiming that a rocket could not work in empty space with nothing to push against, a mistake about the third of these laws. The paper took that claim back in 1969, as Apollo 11 flew to the Moon.
tossups.r: Rockets fly by pushing exhaust backward. For 10 points, name these three laws published by Isaac Newton.

tossups.p: In a classic puzzle, a horse wonders how it can pull a cart if the cart pulls back just as hard; the answer is that the paired forces in the third of these laws act on different objects. A book’s weight and a table’s push on it are not such a pair.
tossups.r: The second of these laws says force equals mass times acceleration. For 10 points, name these three laws stated by Isaac Newton.

tossups.p: The first of these laws overturned Aristotle’s idea that a moving object naturally slows down and stops unless something keeps pushing it. Galileo had paved the way by imagining a ball rolling forever on a perfectly smooth, level surface.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these three laws, which Isaac Newton published in 1687.

tossups.p: A skydiver falling at terminal velocity feels air resistance exactly balance her weight, so by the first of these laws she keeps falling at a steady speed. A free-body diagram shows every force acting on one object so that a student can apply these laws to it.
tossups.r: The second of them says force equals mass times acceleration. For 10 points, name these three laws stated by Isaac Newton.

tossups.p: In a tug-of-war, the rope pulls just as hard on both teams, so the winners are the team that pushes harder against the ground, a lesson in the third of these laws. Walking works the same way: your foot pushes back on the ground, and the ground pushes you forward.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these three laws, the third of which says every action has an equal and opposite reaction.

tossups.p: Edmond Halley paid to print the book that first stated these rules, after the Royal Society said it could not afford to. These rules appear near the start of that book as three “axioms,” written in Latin.
tossups.r: That book, the _Principia_, came out in 1687. For 10 points, name these three laws by Isaac Newton.

tossups.p: These laws stop giving correct answers for objects moving close to the speed of light, where Albert Einstein’s special relativity takes over, and for tiny particles like electrons, which need quantum mechanics.
tossups.r: Still, they work well enough to send spacecraft to the Moon. For 10 points, name these three laws from Isaac Newton’s _Principia_.

tossups.p: Car seatbelts exist because of the first of these laws: in a sudden stop, a passenger’s body keeps moving forward until something stops it. Headrests protect necks in rear-end crashes, when the car lurches forward but the passenger’s head tends to stay behind.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these three laws stated by Isaac Newton, the first of which is called the law of inertia.

tossups.p: The SI unit of force is defined through the second of these laws as the push that makes a one-kilogram mass speed up by one meter per second every second. Doubling the net force on a cart doubles its acceleration, while doubling its mass cuts the acceleration in half.
tossups.r: The unit of force is named for their author. For 10 points, name these three laws from the _Principia_.

tossups.p: A person standing on a bathroom scale in an elevator that is speeding up on its way upward reads heavier than normal, as the second of these laws predicts. An astronaut who throws a wrench in one direction drifts off in the other, as the third of them predicts.
tossups.r: These laws include F equals m a. For 10 points, name these three laws published by Isaac Newton in 1687.

tossups.p: These laws hold exactly only in reference frames that are not accelerating; in a spinning frame, they seem to fail unless you add made-up “fictitious” forces such as the Coriolis force.
tossups.r: The first of them is often called the law of inertia. For 10 points, name these three laws stated by Isaac Newton.

tossups.p: Joseph-Louis Lagrange [“luh-GRAHNJ”] and William Rowan Hamilton later rewrote the physics built on these laws using energy instead of forces. In its general form, the second of these laws says that net force equals the rate at which momentum changes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these three laws of Isaac Newton, which include F equals m a.

tossups.p: A cannon rolls backward when it fires, and a squid jets forward by squirting water out behind it, both examples of the third of these laws. Because of that law, the total momentum of two objects that push only on each other stays the same.
tossups.r: The third of them says every action has an equal and opposite reaction. For 10 points, name these three laws that Isaac Newton published in the _Principia_.

tossups.p: René Descartes [“day-KART”] and Galileo both argued that a moving body keeps moving unless something interferes, an idea that became the first of these laws. That law explains why dishes can stay put when a tablecloth is yanked out from under them.
tossups.r: That first law is also called the law of inertia. For 10 points, name these three laws that Isaac Newton published in 1687.

tossups.p: Combined with a law of universal gravitation, these laws let their author explain Johannes Kepler’s three rules for planetary orbits and work out the paths of comets. Edmond Halley used those ideas to predict the return of the comet now named for him.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these three laws, which include the law of inertia and F equals m a.

clues.t: Three rules, stated by Isaac Newton, that connect forces to the way objects move
First: an object at rest stays at rest, and a moving object keeps moving in a straight line at a steady speed, unless a net force acts on it (the law of inertia)
Second: net force equals mass times acceleration (F = ma)
Third: every action has an equal and opposite reaction, so forces come in pairs
Published in Latin in 1687 in the _Principia_
The two forces in a third-law pair act on different objects, so they never cancel each other out
Rockets, squids, and recoiling cannons move by pushing something the other way (third law)
Walking: your foot pushes back on the ground, and the ground pushes you forward (third law)
Seatbelts and headrests protect riders whose bodies keep moving, or stay behind, when a car suddenly changes speed (first law)
The SI unit of force, named for their author, is defined with the second law: it speeds up 1 kilogram by 1 meter per second every second
Doubling the net force doubles the acceleration; doubling the mass cuts it in half (second law)
The first law overturned Aristotle’s idea that moving things stop unless pushed; Galileo and Descartes paved the way
A skydiver at terminal velocity feels zero net force, so she falls at a steady speed (first law)
The general form of the second law: net force equals the rate of change of momentum; the third law makes momentum conserved
A 1920 newspaper editorial claimed Robert Goddard’s rockets couldn’t work in empty space; the paper took it back in 1969, during Apollo 11
Horse-and-cart puzzle: the cart pulls back as hard as the horse pulls forward, but the paired forces act on different objects
A book’s weight and the table’s upward push are not a third-law pair, since both act on the book
Tug-of-war: the rope pulls equally on both teams, so the winners are the team that pushes harder against the ground
Edmond Halley paid to print the _Principia_ after the Royal Society couldn’t afford it; the laws appear there as three Latin “axioms”
Free-body diagrams show every force on one object so the laws can be applied to it
They hold exactly only in non-accelerating (inertial) frames; spinning frames need fictitious forces like the Coriolis force
They break down near the speed of light (special relativity) and for tiny particles like electrons (quantum mechanics)
Joseph-Louis Lagrange and William Rowan Hamilton later rewrote this physics using energy instead of forces
A scale in an elevator speeding up on its way upward reads heavier (second law); an astronaut who throws a wrench drifts the other way (third law)
With universal gravitation, they explained Kepler’s laws of planetary orbits; Halley used them to predict his comet’s return
The first law explains why dishes can stay put when a tablecloth is yanked out from under them

trap.title: All three, not one
trap.body: These three laws come up as one answer line, but each law can also be its own answer: Newton’s first law (the law of inertia), Newton’s second law (F = ma), and Newton’s third law (action and reaction). If a question asks for “these laws” or “these three laws,” naming just one law, or just “Isaac Newton,” is wrong. Inertia, acceleration, and Newton’s law of universal gravitation are separate answer lines too.
trap.fix: Listen for the pronoun: “these laws” wants the whole set, so say “Newton’s laws of motion”; “this law” wants a single one, so give its number. If the question asks for “this scientist,” the answer is Isaac Newton.
trap.line: Real answer line: Newton’s laws of motion (accept laws of motion; do not accept “Isaac Newton” or a single law)

topics.name: Max Planck
topics.kicker: German father of quantum theory · Energy comes in tiny packets called quanta
topics.briefing: Max Planck was a careful German physicist who started the quantum revolution almost against his will. In 1900, trying to explain the colors of light that hot, glowing objects give off, he proposed that energy is released only in tiny packets, or quanta, whose size is set by a number now called Planck’s constant. He won the 1918 Nobel Prize in Physics, and a European space observatory and dozens of research institutes are named for him.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This physicist later called the key step in his most famous work “an act of desperation,” since he had given up on older physics only reluctantly. He was 42 years old when he took that step.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German physicist whose namesake constant, h, sets the size of a quantum of energy.

tossups.p: As a young student in Munich, this physicist was warned by his teacher Philipp von Jolly that physics was nearly finished, with almost nothing important left to discover. He went on to write his 1879 doctoral thesis on the second law of thermodynamics.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German physicist who won the 1918 Nobel Prize for discovering quanta of energy.

tossups.p: In 1899, this scientist proposed natural units of length, time, and mass built only from basic constants of nature, such as the speed of light and the constant of gravity. The tiny length in that system is about 1.6 times ten to the minus 35 meters.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German physicist who started quantum theory in 1900 and whose constant is symbolized h.

tossups.p: This physicist wrote that a new scientific truth wins not by convincing its opponents, but because its opponents eventually die and a new generation grows up familiar with it. That idea is often shortened to “science advances one funeral at a time.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German physicist who won the 1918 Nobel Prize in Physics for discovering energy quanta.

tossups.p: In the 1930s, this physicist served as president of the Kaiser Wilhelm Society, a group of German research institutes that was refounded under his name in 1948. That society’s institutes have produced many Nobel Prize winners.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this founder of quantum theory, whose namesake constant is about 6.63 times ten to the minus 34 joule-seconds.

tossups.p: The Rayleigh–Jeans law wrongly predicted that a glowing object should give off endless energy at short wavelengths, a failure later nicknamed the “ultraviolet catastrophe.” This physicist’s radiation law avoids that problem and gives the brightness of each color of light from a perfect black body at any temperature.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German physicist who proposed in 1900 that energy is given off in tiny packets called quanta.

tossups.p: This physicist succeeded Gustav Kirchhoff [“KEER-kof”] as a professor of theoretical physics in Berlin, and he later solved the puzzle of “black-body” radiation, a term Kirchhoff had coined. He taught at the University of Berlin from 1889 until 1926.
tossups.r: This physicist’s constant, h, times the frequency of light gives the energy of one photon. For 10 points, name this founder of quantum theory.

tossups.p: From 2009 to 2013, a European Space Agency observatory named for this physicist mapped the cosmic microwave background in great detail, helping pin down the age of the universe at about 13.8 billion years. It was launched together with the Herschel Space Observatory.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German physicist who won the 1918 Nobel Prize in Physics for discovering quanta of energy.

tossups.p: Since 2019, the kilogram has been defined by fixing the exact value of a constant named for this physicist, replacing a metal cylinder kept near Paris. That platinum-iridium cylinder had served as the world’s standard kilogram since 1889.
tossups.r: Multiplying this physicist’s constant by a light wave’s frequency gives the energy of one photon. For 10 points, name this German physicist who founded quantum theory.

tossups.p: This physicist was one of the first famous scientists to support Albert Einstein’s special relativity, and in 1913 he and Walther Nernst [“NAIRNST”] traveled to Zurich to recruit Einstein to Berlin. Einstein moved there the next year.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German physicist who won the 1918 Nobel Prize and whose constant appears in E equals h f.

tossups.p: This physicist’s radiation formula matches Wilhelm Wien’s [“VEENZ”] earlier formula for short wavelengths, but it also works for long ones. Albert Einstein extended this physicist’s idea in 1905, saying that light itself travels in packets, to explain the photoelectric effect.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German physicist whose constant, h, is about 6.63 times ten to the minus 34 joule-seconds.

tossups.p: As a teenager, this future physicist was such a talented pianist that he considered a career in music before choosing physics. He was born in the port city of Kiel in 1858 and grew up in Munich.
tossups.r: Niels Bohr’s 1913 atom used this man’s constant divided by two pi. For 10 points, name this German physicist who founded quantum theory.

tossups.p: Along with Lord Kelvin, this physicist names a statement of the second law of thermodynamics saying that no engine working in a cycle can turn heat entirely into work. He spent his early career studying entropy.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this physicist who proposed in 1900 that energy is given off in tiny packets called quanta.

tossups.p: On December 14, 1900, this physicist explained the reasoning behind his formula for black-body radiation to the German Physical Society in Berlin. That formula matched careful measurements, made by experimenters in Berlin, of the light given off by hot ovens.
tossups.r: That day is often called the birthday of quantum theory. For 10 points, name this German physicist whose constant is h.

tossups.p: Lise Meitner became this physicist’s assistant at the University of Berlin in 1912, at a time when women were rarely given such jobs. His doctoral students included Max von Laue [“LOW-uh”], who later showed that crystals can diffract X-rays.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German physicist who won the 1918 Nobel Prize for discovering energy quanta.

clues.t: German physicist (1858–1947) often called the father of quantum theory
In 1900, proposed that energy is given off in tiny separate packets called quanta
His constant, h (about 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ joule-seconds), times light’s frequency gives the energy of one photon (E = hf)
Won the 1918 Nobel Prize in Physics for discovering energy quanta
Explained black-body radiation, the light given off by a hot, glowing object
His radiation law avoids the “ultraviolet catastrophe” of the Rayleigh–Jeans law, which predicted endless energy at short wavelengths
Einstein extended his idea in 1905, saying light itself comes in packets, to explain the photoelectric effect
Proposed natural units of length, time, and mass (1899), built only from basic constants of nature
The European Space Agency observatory named for him (launched with Herschel) mapped the cosmic microwave background from 2009 to 2013, helping fix the universe’s age at about 13.8 billion years
Since 2019, the kilogram has been defined by fixing his constant’s exact value, replacing a metal cylinder kept near Paris
Bohr’s 1913 atom used his constant divided by 2π (h-bar) for electrons’ angular momentum
Called his quantum idea “an act of desperation,” since he gave up on older physics only reluctantly
Explained the reasoning behind his black-body formula to the German Physical Society on December 14, 1900, often called the birthday of quantum theory
His Munich teacher Philipp von Jolly warned him that physics was nearly finished
Wrote his 1879 doctoral thesis on the second law of thermodynamics and studied entropy early in his career
Shares a statement of the second law with Lord Kelvin: no engine working in a cycle can turn heat entirely into work
Wrote that a new scientific truth wins because its opponents eventually die off, often shortened to “science advances one funeral at a time”
Succeeded Gustav Kirchhoff as a theoretical physics professor in Berlin, where he taught from 1889 to 1926; Kirchhoff had coined the term “black body”
Led the Kaiser Wilhelm Society in the 1930s; it was refounded under his name in 1948
An early supporter of special relativity; in 1913 he and Walther Nernst traveled to Zurich to recruit Einstein to Berlin
A talented teenage pianist who considered a music career; born in Kiel in 1858 and raised in Munich
His radiation formula matches Wilhelm Wien’s earlier formula at short wavelengths but also works at long ones
Lise Meitner became his assistant in Berlin in 1912; his doctoral students included Max von Laue

trap.title: The man, not his constant
trap.body: Many answer lines are named for this man: Planck’s constant, the Planck length, Planck units, and Planck’s law of black-body radiation. If a question asks for “this constant” or “this law,” name the thing; if it asks for “this physicist,” say Planck. Players also mix him up with Albert Einstein, who said in 1905 that light itself comes in packets, and with Max Born, another German-speaking quantum pioneer.
trap.fix: Energy packets in 1900, black-body radiation, the 1918 Nobel Prize, an “act of desperation,” and the Kaiser Wilhelm Society point to Planck. Light quanta and the photoelectric effect in 1905 point to Einstein; the probability meaning of quantum waves points to Max Born.

topics.name: Resonance
topics.kicker: Big vibrations at a natural frequency · How a well-timed push lifts a swing
topics.dates: Studied in sound by Hermann von Helmholtz, 1860s
topics.briefing: Every swing, guitar string, wine glass, and bridge has a natural frequency at which it likes to vibrate. Push it again and again at exactly that rhythm, and the vibrations grow bigger and bigger: that’s resonance. It is why a well-timed push sends a swing soaring, why a powerful singer can shatter a wine glass with one loud note, and why engineers add dampers to keep tall buildings and bridges from swaying dangerously.
topics.answerHtml: Resonance (accept word forms like resonant or resonating; prompt on natural frequency or sympathetic vibration)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: London’s Millennium Bridge closed two days after it opened in 2000, when walkers’ footsteps fell into step with its sideways sway and made it wobble more and more. Engineers fixed that bridge by adding dampers, devices that soak up the energy of this effect.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect in which a system vibrates more and more strongly when it is pushed at its natural frequency.

tossups.p: The 1940 collapse of the Tacoma Narrows Bridge, nicknamed “Galloping Gertie,” is often blamed on this effect, although engineers say the true cause was a related twisting motion called aeroelastic flutter. That bridge in Washington State twisted wildly in a steady wind just four months after it opened.
tossups.r: This effect lets a well-timed push send a playground swing higher and higher. For 10 points, name this effect, in which a system is driven at its natural frequency.

tossups.p: England’s Broughton Suspension Bridge, near Manchester, collapsed in 1831 while a column of soldiers marched across it in step. Afterward, the British Army began ordering troops to break step when crossing bridges, to avoid this effect.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, in which repeated pushes at an object’s natural frequency make its vibrations grow larger and larger.

tossups.p: Daniel Kirkwood found gaps in the asteroid belt where an asteroid would circle the Sun, for example, exactly three times for every one orbit of Jupiter, a gravitational case of this effect. Saturn’s moon Mimas [“MY-mus”] helps clear the Cassini Division in Saturn’s rings in the same way.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, which also lets a singer shatter a wine glass by singing its natural pitch.

tossups.p: Hermann von Helmholtz used hollow spheres with two openings, each built to respond to a single pitch, to pick out the notes hidden inside a sound through this effect. Blowing across the top of an empty bottle makes it hum by the same effect.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect that lets a powerful singer shatter a wine glass by matching its natural frequency.

tossups.p: Turning a radio’s tuning dial adjusts a circuit of an inductor and a capacitor so that this effect happens at the frequency of just one station. In such a circuit, energy sloshes back and forth between the inductor and the capacitor at their natural rate.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, in which a system responds strongly to pushes at its own natural frequency.

tossups.p: A system’s “Q factor” tells how sharp and long-lasting this effect is, so a high-Q tuning fork rings for a long time after it is struck. Damping, such as friction, lowers and widens the peak on a graph of this effect.
tossups.r: The letter R in MRI stands for a magnetic form of this effect. For 10 points, name this effect, in which a system vibrates strongly at its natural frequency.

tossups.p: Quartz watches keep time with a tiny crystal that vibrates 32,768 times per second, the rate at which this effect makes the crystal ring most strongly when an electric circuit pushes on it. That number is two to the fifteenth power.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, in which pushing an object at its natural frequency makes it vibrate strongly, as when a swing is pushed in rhythm.

tossups.p: The “ocean” you hear when you hold a seashell to your ear is really background noise boosted by this effect inside the shell’s hollow space. The hollow body of an acoustic guitar uses this effect to make the strings’ sound louder.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, in which an object vibrates strongly when pushed at its natural frequency.

tossups.p: In a classic lab, students hold a humming tuning fork over a tube of water and raise or lower the water until the sound suddenly gets loud, showing this effect in the air column. Striking one tuning fork can make an identical fork nearby start humming on its own.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, in which a system vibrates especially strongly when pushed at its natural frequency.

tossups.p: The Taipei 101 skyscraper hangs a giant steel ball near its top as a tuned mass damper, which sways against the building to fight this effect during typhoons and earthquakes. Tall buildings are designed so that their natural sway does not match the shaking they are likely to face.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect in which a system shakes harder and harder when pushed at its natural frequency.

tossups.p: A sitar has extra strings that the player usually leaves unplucked; they ring by this effect when the played strings sound their notes. Holding down a piano’s sustain pedal and singing loudly into the piano makes its strings answer back by the same effect.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, in which vibrations at an object’s natural frequency make it vibrate strongly.

tossups.p: The vowel sounds of human speech come from peaks called formants, which this effect creates in the throat and mouth. Changing the shape of your mouth changes which pitches this effect boosts, which is how you can tell an “ee” from an “oo.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, which lets a singer break a wine glass with the right note.

tossups.p: Pluto circles the Sun twice for every three orbits of Neptune, and Jupiter’s moons Io, Europa, and Ganymede are locked in a 1:2:4 pattern; both are orbital examples of this effect. The pattern between Pluto and Neptune keeps the two from ever coming close, even though their orbits seem to cross.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, in which a swing goes higher when pushed in rhythm with its natural frequency.

tossups.p: Cesium atomic clocks keep time by adjusting microwaves until cesium atoms respond most strongly, at a rate of about 9.19 billion vibrations per second that has defined the second since 1967. Your ear canal boosts sounds near 3,000 hertz by the same effect.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, which lets a well-timed push send a child on a swing higher.

clues.t: When a system is pushed again and again at its natural frequency, its vibrations grow larger and larger
Pushing a swing in rhythm with its natural frequency sends it higher and higher
A powerful singer can shatter a wine glass by loudly singing its natural pitch
Striking one tuning fork can make an identical fork nearby start humming on its own
Soldiers break step on bridges, a rule adopted after England’s Broughton Suspension Bridge, near Manchester, collapsed under marching troops in 1831
Often blamed for the 1940 Tacoma Narrows Bridge (“Galloping Gertie”) collapse, though aeroelastic flutter was the true cause
London’s Millennium Bridge wobbled and closed two days after opening in 2000; dampers fixed it
Tuning a radio adjusts an inductor–capacitor circuit so it responds to just one station’s frequency
The R in MRI stands for a magnetic version of it in atomic nuclei
A guitar’s hollow body makes the strings louder, and a seashell’s “ocean sound” is background noise boosted inside it
Classic lab: raise or lower the water in a tube under a humming tuning fork until the air column suddenly booms
Damping, such as friction, lowers and widens its peak; tuned mass dampers fight it in skyscrapers
Daniel Kirkwood’s gaps in the asteroid belt come from orbital versions caused by Jupiter, such as three asteroid orbits per Jupiter orbit
Saturn’s moon Mimas helps clear the Cassini Division in Saturn’s rings this way
Pluto orbits twice for every three Neptune orbits, which keeps them from ever coming close; Io, Europa, and Ganymede are locked in a 1:2:4 pattern
Hermann von Helmholtz used hollow spheres, each tuned to one pitch, to pick out the notes in a sound; blowing across a bottle works the same way
The Q factor measures how sharp and long-lasting it is; a high-Q tuning fork rings a long time
Quartz watch crystals vibrate 32,768 times per second (2 to the 15th power)
Taipei 101 hangs a giant steel ball near its top as a tuned mass damper
A sitar’s extra strings, usually left unplucked, ring through it, and so do a piano’s strings when you sing into it with the sustain pedal down
Vowel sounds come from peaks called formants, made by it in the throat and mouth
Cesium atomic clocks tune microwaves until the atoms respond most strongly, about 9.19 billion times per second, the rate that has defined the second since 1967
The ear canal boosts sounds near 3,000 hertz this way

trap.title: Effect, not frequency
trap.body: Resonance is the effect; the natural (or resonant) frequency is just the special frequency at which it happens, so “natural frequency” earns only a prompt and plain “frequency” is wrong. Clues about strings, organ pipes, and tuning forks can also tempt players into “harmonics” or “standing waves,” and a siren’s changing pitch is the Doppler effect, not this.
trap.fix: Vibrations that grow from well-timed pushes, shattered wine glasses, swings, swaying bridges, dampers, and tuned radios mean resonance. The special frequency itself is the natural frequency; patterns of nodes on a string are standing waves; and a moving source’s pitch shift is the Doppler effect.
trap.line: Real answer line: Resonance (accept word forms like resonant or resonating; prompt on natural frequency or sympathetic vibration)

topics.name: X-rays
topics.kicker: Invisible high-energy rays that pass through skin · Found by Röntgen, 1895
topics.briefing: In November 1895, the German physicist Wilhelm Röntgen noticed a screen glowing across his darkened lab while he ran electricity through a glass tube wrapped in black cardboard. The invisible rays causing the glow could pass through skin and paper but not bone or metal, and he named them X-rays, with the X standing for “unknown.” Doctors use X-rays to find broken bones, dentists use them to find cavities, and space telescopes use them to study black holes and exploding stars.
topics.answerHtml: X-rays (accept X-radiation or Röntgen rays; prompt on electromagnetic radiation; do not accept “gamma rays”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Hospital tubes make these rays when fast electrons slam into a metal target such as tungsten and give off “braking radiation,” or Bremsstrahlung [“BREMS-shtrah-lung”], as they slow down. In 1913, William Coolidge improved those tubes by using a heated filament to supply the electrons.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these rays, discovered by Wilhelm Röntgen, that doctors use to see broken bones.

tossups.p: William Henry Bragg and his son Lawrence shared the 1915 Nobel Prize in Physics for bouncing these rays off crystals to work out where the atoms sit; Lawrence was only 25 years old. Max von Laue [“LOW-uh”] had shown in 1912 that crystals diffract these rays.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these rays, which lie between ultraviolet light and gamma rays on the electromagnetic spectrum.

tossups.p: In 1913, Henry Moseley [“MOHZ-lee”] measured these rays given off by different elements and showed that the periodic table should be ordered by atomic number. His method worked because each element gives off these rays at its own set of wavelengths.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these rays that pass through skin but are blocked by bone.

tossups.p: Arthur Compton won a Nobel Prize after showing in 1923 that these rays bounce off electrons like billiard balls, coming out with longer wavelengths. That result helped convince physicists that light is made of particles called photons.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these high-energy rays, which Wilhelm Röntgen discovered in 1895.

tossups.p: NASA’s Chandra observatory, carried into orbit in 1999 on the first space shuttle mission commanded by a woman, Eileen Collins, studies these rays from space, since Earth’s atmosphere blocks them. Chandra’s mirrors are nearly parallel to the incoming rays, because these rays reflect only at very shallow angles.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this kind of high-energy radiation that dentists use to look for cavities.

tossups.p: Godfrey Hounsfield and Allan Cormack shared the 1979 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for computed tomography, or CT, which combines many images made with these rays into slices of the body.
tossups.r: On ordinary images made with these rays, bones show up white. For 10 points, name these rays, which doctors use to check for broken bones.

tossups.p: One of the first images ever made with these rays showed the hand of the discoverer’s wife, wedding ring and all. Their discoverer won the first Nobel Prize in Physics, in 1901.
tossups.r: He named them with an X because they were unknown. For 10 points, name these rays found by Wilhelm Röntgen in 1895.

tossups.p: Before some scans with these rays, patients swallow a chalky drink of barium sulfate, which blocks the rays and makes the stomach and intestines show up clearly. Technicians cover other parts of the body with aprons containing lead, which also blocks them.
tossups.r: Bones look white on images made with these rays. For 10 points, name these rays discovered by Wilhelm Röntgen.

tossups.p: Riccardo Giacconi [“jah-KOH-nee”] won the 2002 Nobel Prize in Physics for founding the astronomy of these rays, which took off when his team’s rocket found the source Scorpius X-1 in 1962. That source turned out to be a neutron star pulling gas off a companion star.
tossups.r: Hot gas around black holes and neutron stars gives off these rays. For 10 points, name this type of radiation that can pass through skin and muscle.

tossups.p: From the 1920s to the 1950s, many shoe stores used “shoe-fitting fluoroscopes,” machines that used these rays to let customers look right through new shoes to see how their feet fit. Worries about radiation ended that practice.
tossups.r: Large doses of these rays can damage DNA. For 10 points, name these rays that doctors use to look at bones.

tossups.p: Higher-energy “hard” types of these rays pass through more material than lower-energy “soft” ones. These rays have shorter wavelengths than ultraviolet light, about the size of the gaps between atoms, which is why they are useful for studying crystals.
tossups.r: Element 111, roentgenium, honors their discoverer. For 10 points, name these rays used to photograph bones.

tossups.p: Rosalind Franklin’s “Photo 51,” made by sending these rays through fibers of DNA, showed an X-shaped pattern that revealed the molecule’s helix shape. Dorothy Hodgkin used these rays to work out the structures of penicillin and vitamin B12.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these rays, used in crystallography, that Wilhelm Röntgen discovered in 1895.

tossups.p: While running a glass tube wrapped in black cardboard in Würzburg [“VURTS-burg”], a physicist noticed a screen coated with barium platinocyanide glowing across the room one day in November, the first sign of these rays.
tossups.r: His paper “On a New Kind of Rays” announced them at the end of 1895. For 10 points, name these rays discovered by Wilhelm Röntgen.

tossups.p: Mammograms, which help doctors find breast cancer early, use low doses of these rays. Like gamma rays, these rays are “ionizing,” meaning they carry enough energy to knock electrons off atoms, so patients are exposed to them only when needed.
tossups.r: Dentists use them to find cavities. For 10 points, name these rays that pass through skin but not bone.

tossups.p: Thomas Edison built devices called fluoroscopes that used these rays in 1896, but he gave up the work after his assistant Clarence Dally became seriously ill from exposure to them.
tossups.r: The comic-book hero Superman has a kind of vision named for these rays. For 10 points, name these rays discovered by Wilhelm Röntgen.

clues.t: Discovered by the German physicist Wilhelm Röntgen in 1895
Named with an X because Röntgen did not know what they were: X stands for “unknown”
Pass through skin and muscle but are blocked by bone and metal, so doctors use them to see broken bones; bones look white on the images
Electromagnetic waves with shorter wavelengths than ultraviolet light; gamma rays lie beyond them
Dentists use them to find cavities, and mammograms use low doses of them
Their discoverer won the first Nobel Prize in Physics, in 1901
One of the first images showed the hand of Röntgen’s wife, wedding ring and all
Lead aprons block them; a chalky barium sulfate drink makes the stomach and intestines show up
CT (computed tomography) scans combine many images into slices; Hounsfield and Cormack won the 1979 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine
Ionizing: they carry enough energy to knock electrons off atoms, and large doses can damage DNA
Earth’s atmosphere blocks them, so telescopes that study them must be in space
Max von Laue (1912) showed that crystals diffract them; crystallography uses them to find where atoms sit
Superman has a kind of vision named for them
William Henry Bragg and his son Lawrence shared the 1915 Nobel Prize for studying crystals with them; Lawrence was 25
Henry Moseley (1913) used the ones given off by different elements to order the periodic table by atomic number
Arthur Compton (1923): they bounce off electrons like billiard balls and come out with longer wavelengths
NASA’s Chandra observatory (1999) was launched on Eileen Collins’s shuttle mission; its mirrors reflect them only at very shallow angles
Riccardo Giacconi founded their astronomy; his team’s rocket found Scorpius X-1 in 1962, and he won the 2002 Nobel Prize
Made when fast electrons slam into a metal target like tungsten and give off “braking radiation” (Bremsstrahlung)
William Coolidge’s 1913 tube used a heated filament to supply the electrons
Rosalind Franklin’s “Photo 51” revealed DNA’s helix shape; Dorothy Hodgkin used them to solve penicillin and vitamin B12
Thomas Edison built fluoroscopes using them in 1896, but quit after his assistant Clarence Dally became seriously ill from exposure
From the 1920s to the 1950s, shoe stores used shoe-fitting fluoroscopes that let customers see through new shoes to check the fit
Element 111, roentgenium, honors their discoverer
“Hard” (higher-energy) ones pass through more material than “soft” ones; their wavelengths are about the size of the gaps between atoms
Röntgen saw a barium platinocyanide screen glow in Würzburg and announced the rays in “On a New Kind of Rays” (end of 1895)

trap.title: Not gamma or cathode rays
trap.body: X-rays and gamma rays are both invisible, high-energy light that can pass through matter, and their energies overlap. Gamma rays usually come from atomic nuclei, as in radioactive decay, while X-rays usually come from electrons, like those slamming into a metal target in a hospital tube. Cathode rays, which Röntgen was studying when he found X-rays, are streams of electrons, not light at all.
trap.fix: Broken bones, dentists, Röntgen, crystals, the Braggs, Moseley, CT scans, and the Chandra telescope point to X-rays. Radioactive nuclei and Paul Villard (who found them in 1900) point to gamma rays, and a beam of electrons inside a glass tube is cathode rays.
trap.line: Real answer line: X-rays (accept X-radiation or Röntgen rays; prompt on electromagnetic radiation; do not accept “gamma rays”)
